name: LongFact
summary: 2,280 fact-seeking prompts across 38 topics that ask for long, detailed answers, for measuring the factuality of long-form responses.
overview:
LongFact tests the factual accuracy of long-form answers. Many factuality benchmarks ask about a single fact with a short answer; LongFact prompts instead ask a model to explain a concept or describe a specific person, place, event, or other object in detail, which calls for several paragraphs containing many facts. It has two tasks over the same 38 topics, grouped into STEM, social sciences, humanities, and other. LongFact-Concepts asks about general ideas such as theories, doctrines, and methods. LongFact-Objects, the main task, asks about specific entities, which the authors describe as harder because models usually know less about niche entities. [Original paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.18802) and [LongFact README](https://github.com/google-deepmind/long-form-factuality/blob/9d27158d198ced0a9d8271a80147cae580614601/longfact/README.md)

The authors chose the topics by hand and had GPT-4 write the prompts one at a time. Each request included ten example prompts, starting from ten the authors wrote and gradually replaced by generated ones to increase variety. They generated 60 prompts per topic and task, removed by hand any questions in the same topic that could be answered with about the same response, and randomly kept 30. LongFact was introduced in March 2024 alongside SAFE, an automated method for rating long-form responses, and the F1@K metric. [Original paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.18802)
methodology:
This snapshot contains all 2,280 prompts at the pinned commit: 1,140 from LongFact-Concepts and 1,140 from LongFact-Objects, 30 for each of the 38 topics. They come from the two folders whose names end in noduplicates, one JSONL file per topic. The SAFE evaluator, experiment code, and model responses in the repository are not imported. [LongFact folder](https://github.com/google-deepmind/long-form-factuality/tree/9d27158d198ced0a9d8271a80147cae580614601/longfact)

Each Task Prompt is the upstream prompt verbatim, which is the text sent to the model under evaluation. LongFact has no reference answers, so tasks have no Solution. Every upstream record also carries the same canary string asking that benchmark data stay out of training corpora; the importer checks it, and the redistribution review records it.

IDs are the task, the topic as named in the upstream file in lowercase, and the two-digit line number, such as objects-astronomy-01 or concepts-us-foreign-policy-30. Nine LongFact-Objects prompts, such as Who is Louis Pasteur?, appear in two topics, mostly clinical knowledge and medicine, because duplicates were removed within each topic; each copy keeps its own ID. Source links point to the prompt's line in the pinned topic file. No task-specific software environment is required. The importer uses only Python's standard library and can be rerun with python3 data/longfact/import.py.
scoring:
Responses are rated with SAFE (Search-Augmented Factuality Evaluator). A language model splits the response into individual facts, rewrites each to be self-contained, and drops facts that are irrelevant to the prompt. For each remaining fact it issues Google Search queries over several steps and decides whether the results support the fact. SAFE reports the numbers of supported, not-supported, and irrelevant facts. The paper's configuration uses GPT-3.5-Turbo with the Serper search API, five search steps, and three results per query. [Original paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.18802) and [evaluation code](https://github.com/google-deepmind/long-form-factuality/tree/9d27158d198ced0a9d8271a80147cae580614601/eval)

The paper combines these counts with F1@K. Precision is the share of supported facts among supported and not-supported facts. Recall is the number of supported facts divided by K, capped at 1, where K stands for a preferred number of facts in a response. F1@K is their harmonic mean, or 0 when no fact is supported. The paper benchmarks thirteen models on the same random 250 LongFact-Objects prompts, decoding up to 1,024 tokens at temperature zero, and reports F1@64 and F1@178. Those values of K are the median and maximum numbers of relevant facts among the responses tested. [Original paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.18802)

Compare results that use the same prompts, rater model, search backend, and K. Benchopedia stores the published prompts. It does not run evaluations or publish model scores for this snapshot.
limitations:
GPT-4 wrote the prompts, so their quality and topic fit depend on that model, and the topics and phrasing reflect its choices. There are no reference answers: scores depend on an automated rater and on what Google Search returns, which can change over time and may lack depth in expert domains such as law and medicine. The paper reports that SAFE agreed with crowdsourced annotators on 72% of about 16,000 facts and was judged correct in 76% of 100 sampled disagreements, so ratings still contain errors. F1@K assumes a response does not repeat facts, and the paper notes that repeating a supported fact could inflate the score. [Original paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.18802)

The prompts are public, so a score alone cannot establish that a model was tested on unseen material. [LongFact folder](https://github.com/google-deepmind/long-form-factuality/tree/9d27158d198ced0a9d8271a80147cae580614601/longfact)
